sections.title: Overview

summary.text: Gives an overview of the technical brief, which updates WHO guidance to support differentiated, simplified, demedicalized PrEP services in line with the 2022–2030 global health sector strategies. It lists key points on starting and stopping oral PrEP, including event-driven dosing for people assigned male at birth not taking estradiol-based hormones, and on hepatitis B and C testing. It also introduces the four building blocks of differentiated delivery: where, who, when and what.

sections.extract: What is this technical brief? This technical brief by the World Health Organization (WHO) updates and supplements previous WHO guidelines and guidance on pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention. The brief aims to support differentiated, simplified, demedicalized and comprehensive PrEP services. This can support PrEP uptake, persistence and effective use and assist efforts to achieve global goals set out

sections.title: Background

summary.text: Explains what PrEP is and recalls that WHO's 2015 recommendation of TDF-based oral PrEP was cautious because experience was limited, whereas services have since been widely simplified, demedicalized and integrated. It states the brief's aim of supporting these trends, accelerated by COVID-19, towards the UN target of fewer than 370 000 new infections by 2025, and summarises WHO PrEP recommendations in a box.

sections.extract: Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention is the use of antiretroviral drugs by HIV-negative individuals to reduce the risk of acquisition of HIV. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended multiple PrEP options as part of combination prevention approaches (Box 1). When WHO recommended offering TDF-based oral PrEP to people at substantial risk for HIV in 2015 (Box 2), implementation of PrEP

sections.title: Target audience and scope

summary.text: Describes the brief's audience and scope: it supplements WHO consolidated HIV guidelines and the PrEP Implementation Tool, focusing on TDF-based oral PrEP while noting considerations for the dapivirine vaginal ring and long-acting cabotegravir.

sections.extract: This technical brief aims to support a range of stakeholders in planning and implementing PrEP services. It provides guidance on PrEP implementation and is meant to supplement and update guidance previously published in the WHO Consolidated HIV Guidelines (4) and the WHO PrEP Implementation Tool.3 The guidance in this document relates primarily to TDF-based oral PrEP (including TDF in combination with emtricitabine

sections.title: Guiding principle and methodology

summary.text: Describes the brief's people-centred, rights-based approach and how it was developed by a WHO core group with an expert working group, including management of declarations of interest. It also begins guidance that eligible people assigned male at birth may choose event-driven or daily oral PrEP, with a footnote defining transgender people.

sections.extract: This technical brief follows a public health, human rights and people-centred approach to provide evidence-based guidance on PrEP service delivery. Such an approach puts the people and communities who could benefit from PrEP services at the centre of service delivery, adapting services to their preferences and needs while maximizing impact and health system efficiency. sections.title: Starting and stopping oral PrEP

summary.text: Sets out how to start and stop oral PrEP: people eligible for event-driven PrEP take a double loading dose 2–24 hours before sex and continue daily until two days after the last exposure. All other groups, including cisgender women and people who inject drugs, take seven daily doses before protection and stop seven days after the last exposure. A figure illustrates the dosing timelines.

sections.extract: To reduce the risk of HIV acquisition through sexual exposure, cisgender men and trans and gender diverse people assigned male at birth4 who are not taking exogenous estradiol-based hormones may be offered oral daily PrEP or ED-PrEP as options (Table 1 and Figure 1). Whether the intention is to use oral daily PrEP or ED-PrEP, people eligible for ED-PrEP can start and stop PrEP using the same strategy: • Start PrEP

sections.title: Rationale

summary.text: Explains the evidence that event-driven PrEP is as effective as daily PrEP for cisgender men who have sex with men and why it can be extended to all people assigned male at birth not taking estradiol-based hormones, regardless of sexual positioning. It notes insufficient evidence for other groups and compares lead-in and stopping times recommended in other guidelines.

sections.extract: Data from trials, open label extension studies and demonstration studies have shown that oral PrEP using the ED-PrEP dosing regimen is as effective in preventing HIV infection as daily PrEP in cisgender men who have sex with men (6–8). sections.title: PrEP and hepatitis B and C

summary.text: Gives a flowchart-style summary of hepatitis B management in PrEP services: vaccination for those testing HBsAg-negative and assessment for treatment for those positive. It explains that TDF-based PrEP also suppresses hepatitis B, notes the small risk of relapse after stopping and the need for monitoring.

sections.title: Hepatitis B virus

summary.text: Recommends testing PrEP users once for hepatitis B surface antigen, especially in highly endemic countries, while stressing that lack of testing must not delay PrEP. It notes that oral PrEP and the dapivirine ring are safe for people with hepatitis B or C and repeats the key points on hepatitis testing.

sections.extract: Testing PrEP users for HBsAg once, at or within one to three months of PrEP initiation (or later if not available around initiation), is strongly encouraged, particularly in highly endemic countries. TDF-based daily or event- driven oral PrEP and the DVR can be safely offered to persons with HBV infection. There are specific considerations regarding offering CAB-LA to people with HBV (Box 3). sections.title: Hepatitis C virus

summary.text: Recommends hepatitis C antibody testing at PrEP start and yearly for populations at high risk, while making clear that testing is not a requirement for PrEP. It covers referral for treatment, HCV self-testing and specific considerations for long-acting cabotegravir in people with hepatitis C.

sections.extract: HCV antibody testing is strongly encouraged at or within one to three months of PrEP initiation (or later if not available around initiation), and every 12 months thereafter, where PrEP services are provided to populations at high risk of HCV infection. Risks of HCV vary across settings, and populations at high risk of HCV include, but are not limited to, cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men,

sections.title: Rationale

summary.text: Explains the rationale for the hepatitis guidance, citing global estimates of hepatitis B and C burden and the 2030 elimination goal. It revises earlier advice by stating that hepatitis B infection does not rule out event-driven PrEP, because clinical relapse is rare, and discusses PrEP choices for pregnant people living with hepatitis B.

sections.extract: WHO estimates that in 2019, there were 296 million people living with chronic HBV infection and 58 million people living with HCV infection worldwide (31). An estimated 1.1 million deaths in 2019 were due to HBV and HCV infection. The Global Health Sector Strategy on Viral Hepatitis, approved by the World Health Assembly in 2016, set the goal to eliminate viral hepatitis as a major public health threat by 2030 (32).

sections.title: PrEP and kidney function

summary.text: Sets out guidance on kidney function and TDF-based oral PrEP: impaired kidney function is a contraindication, but testing is optional for people under 30 without comorbidities and can be limited for others. It advises that waiting for results should not delay PrEP and that tests be repeated before stopping. Notes cover estimating kidney function, including during pregnancy and gender-affirming hormone use.

sections.extract: Impaired kidney function, indicated by an eGFR of <60 mL/min per 1.73 m2 or an estimated creatinine clearance of <60 mL/min, is a contraindication for the use of TDF-based oral PrEP. Measuring kidney function in potential PrEP users at initiation and during PrEP continuation is suggested for some populations. sections.title: Rationale

summary.text: Explains the rationale for reduced kidney testing, citing meta-analyses showing mostly mild, reversible kidney effects and data from over 18 000 people screened in which abnormal values were rare and increased with age.

sections.extract: Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) found that individuals taking TDF-based oral PrEP have, on average, a higher risk of experiencing kidney-related adverse events compared with individuals taking placebos (46–48), but these adverse events tend to be mild, nonprogressive, and reversible after PrEP discontinuation. sections.title: HIVST and PrEP

summary.text: Describes how HIV self-testing can support PrEP, drawing on COVID-19 experience and a review showing fewer clinic visits and testing between visits. It outlines three uses—demand generation and linkage, PrEP initiation, and continuation—and notes the need for community engagement and further operational research.

sections.extract: HIVST could be an important tool to enable countries to increase access to PrEP and uptake, persistence and effective use. Since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, WHO has supported HIVST to maintain PrEP services (51), and several countries have integrated HIVST into their PrEP programming to initiate and continue clients on PrEP (see Box 6 and 10 in next section). A literature review found evidence that HIVST

sections.title: What is HIVST?

summary.text: Explains what HIV self-testing is, its WHO recommendation since 2016 and the prequalified products available. It discusses using self-testing to start PrEP outside clinics despite limited evidence, addressing concerns about acute infection and drug resistance. Modelling summarised here suggests that self-testing may miss some infections but that drug-resistance prevalence stays similar across scenarios.

sections.extract: In HIVST, people collect their own specimen (generally oral fluid or fingerprick whole blood) using a simple rapid HIV test and then perform the test and interpret their result, often in private or with someone they trust. WHO has recommended HIVST as an approach to HIV testing services since 2016 (4), and the approach has been scaled up globally with nearly 100 countries reporting national policies.6 Currently,

sections.title: Rationale

summary.text: Summarises a systematic review of self-testing for PrEP, including a Kenyan trial in which six-month dispensing with self-testing halved clinic visits without reducing persistence.

sections.extract: A systematic review on HIVST for PrEP initiation and continuation (52) identified three completed RCTs that evaluated PrEP continuation after initiation in health care facilities, while no studies evaluated HIVST-based PrEP initiation. sections.title: Building blocks of differentiated PrEP service delivery

summary.text: Introduces differentiated PrEP delivery, noting the shift away from clinic-only physician prescribing that accelerated during COVID-19.

sections.extract: delivery In many countries, individuals interested in PrEP must go to a health care facility (often an HIV clinic) to obtain a prescription from a medical provider (often a physician). In recent years, and particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic (60), the shift towards differentiated PrEP service delivery has accelerated.

sections.title: Differentiated PrEP service delivery: When, where, who and what to deliver

summary.text: Defines differentiated PrEP service delivery as person- and community-centred and links it to the global health sector strategies. It presents the four building blocks (when, where, who and what), which can differ between initiation, continuation and re-initiation and across PrEP products.

sections.extract: delivery: When, where, who and what to deliver A differentiated PrEP service delivery approach is person- and community-centred and adapts services to the needs and preferences of the people who are interested in and could benefit from PrEP. Differentiated PrEP service delivery may also support more efficient and cost–effective use of health care resources. WHO recommends differentiated service delivery for HIV

sections.title: Where to deliver PrEP

summary.text: Sets out barriers to PrEP in health facilities, such as stigma, lack of privacy, distance, costs and long waits, as well as provider-side barriers. It argues that oral PrEP and the ring have few required components and can be delivered in community settings, while more research is needed for long-acting cabotegravir. Evidence and provider views on community-based delivery follow.

sections.extract: There are a range of barriers to PrEP access, uptake, persistence and effective use associated with service delivery in health care facilities. These include actual or perceived lack of privacy, stigma and discrimination, negative attitudes of health care providers, travel distance, direct and opportunity costs for clients, frequency of required clinic visits for continuation, lengthy waiting times and inconvenient

sections.title: PrEP in fixed and mobile community settings

summary.text: Describes oral PrEP delivery in fixed and mobile community sites, such as NGO centres and vans, and the importance of partnerships with community organizations and integrated services. A box summarises review evidence, including the SEARCH trial in Kenya and Uganda and the Love O2O study in Thailand, and an example from Viet Nam is pictured.

sections.extract: Service models that deliver oral PrEP in fixed community sites (such as through nongovernmental organizations) and mobile and semimobile sites (for example, vans parked in community settings) have been implemented. A systematic review (Box 7) (63) identified diverse models demonstrating the feasibility of these approaches in a range of countries, but data on effectiveness were limited. In addition to considerations

sections.title: Telehealth for PrEP

summary.text: Describes telehealth platforms for delivering PrEP, which WHO supports as an additional option provided data security and confidentiality are protected. It lists aspects of service delivery that telehealth can support, such as risk assessment, home delivery of self-test kits and prescriptions. Evidence from case studies and ongoing US trials is summarised, with a photo from a Brazilian project.

sections.extract: The use of information and telecommunication technologies to create virtual platforms for delivering PrEP services has the potential to remove barriers to PrEP uptake and persistence and support effective use of PrEP. WHO recommends that online delivery of HIV, viral hepatitis and STI services to key populations may be offered as an additional option, while ensuring that data security and confidentiality are

sections.title: PrEP delivery in pharmacies

summary.text: Explains that pharmacies can be more accessible and convenient than clinics and may expand PrEP access, though effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of pharmacy delivery remain unknown. It sets out what pharmacists need, such as legal authority, testing infrastructure and training, and cites Kenyan experience showing similar uptake and persistence, noting that legal changes are needed for pharmacists to prescribe PrEP.

sections.extract: Pharmacies can be more accessible, acceptable and convenient for clients than health care facilities. In resource-limited settings, individuals commonly first seek health care services from pharmacies before going to clinics (72,73). The WHO Guideline on Self- Care Interventions for Health and Well-Being (74) notes that providing PrEP through pharmacies may present an opportunity to expand access to PrEP. However,

sections.title: Who to deliver PrEP

summary.text: Contrasts WHO task-sharing recommendations for ART with PrEP, which in most countries is prescribed by clinicians while lay providers handle other tasks such as risk assessment and HIV testing. It argues that sharing PrEP tasks with peers and community health workers may improve efficiency and acceptability, noting research needs for long-acting cabotegravir and requirements for training, quality assurance, clinical oversight and fair pay.

sections.extract: For HIV treatment, WHO recommends (4) that 1) trained nonphysician clinicians, nurses and midwives can initiate and maintain ART, and 2) trained and supervised community health workers can dispense ART and lay providers can distribute ART. sections.title: When and what services to deliver

summary.text: Discusses when and what PrEP services to deliver, starting with multi-month dispensing, which is standard for ART and is being adapted for PrEP after an initial one-month visit, with examples from Viet Nam, Zimbabwe and a Kenyan trial of six-month dispensing with HIV self-testing. It then covers integrating PrEP with other services, such as gender-affirming care, harm reduction, antenatal and family planning services, and a status-neutral approach to testing. It ends with a case study from Glasgow on PrEP for people who inject drugs, where staffing intensity limits expansion.

sections.extract: Multi-month dispensing (MMD) WHO recommends that people living with HIV established on ART should be offered three-to-six– month ART refills, preferably lasting six months (4). MMD of ART has been found to be feasible and cost- saving for providers and clients in a range of countries, and COVID-19 has accelerated adoption of ART MMD (83). For oral PrEP, a one-month supply is commonly provided at initiation,

sections.title: Research gaps

summary.text: Identifies research gaps for differentiated PrEP delivery, calling for implementation science and quasi-experimental methods to measure effects on uptake, persistence and effective use. It notes that evidence is concentrated among men who have sex with men and young women in a few countries, and that experience with the dapivirine ring and long-acting cabotegravir is still lacking.

sections.extract: While the feasibility of a range of differentiated PrEP service delivery models has been demonstrated, additional evidence of effectiveness of PrEP-related outcomes (uptake, persistence and effective use) is needed. sections.title: Annex 1: Summary of mathematical modelling of HIVST for PrEP in Kenya

summary.text: Annex 1, summarizing mathematical modelling of HIV self-testing for community-based oral PrEP delivery in Kenya. It concludes that expanding PrEP could avert nearly half of new infections over 20 years and that self-testing-based delivery could be effective, with only small increases in inappropriate PrEP use and drug resistance compared with provider testing.

sections.title: Annex 2: Background and methods on the global PrEP provider study

summary.text: Annex 2, describing the methods of a WHO-supported global survey and in-depth interviews of PrEP providers carried out between November 2021 and February 2022 on service practices and views of new PrEP products. It explains how questions were developed and translated and lists participating providers by WHO region and country.

sections.extract: methods on the global PrEP provider study WHO supported a global study of PrEP providers, comprising an online survey and in-depth interviews, from November 2021 through February 2022. The survey aimed to understand current service delivery practices as well as perspectives on new PrEP products. sections.title: Annex 3: Summary of a review of PrEP services for people who inject drugs

summary.text: Annex 3, summarizing a review of PrEP services for people who inject drugs, which found limited availability and use. It recommends expanding PrEP within harm reduction programmes, preferably community-based and peer-led, and lists service models found, before ending with WHO's contact details.
